text:
B: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
A: Yes. Hello. Yeah, I can hear you.
B: Champion. I'm Craig, I'm in Lancaster.
A: Tomasz. I'm in Exeter.
B: Exeter, nice. Long way down. I clocked the Dartmoor map in your picture. Do you get up there much?
A: Erm, yeah. Quite a lot. Most weekends, if I'm not on shift.
B: On shift where, if you don't mind me asking?
A: Food factory, on the edge of Exeter. I'm machine operator on a packing line. And I'm also student, sorry, I mean I'm a student as well. Archaeology. Second year.
B: Both at once? That must be knackering.
A: It is, yeah. Last week one machine kept jamming all night, I got home at six and had seminar at ten. So.
B: Oof. Did you make it?
A: I made it. I didn't say anything, but I made it.
B: Fair play. I tried uni, actually. Outdoor education, up in Cumbria. Lasted a year, then I couldn't afford it and I just sort of felt like I didn't fit, you know. Went and fixed bikes instead.
A: Mm. I did one year of history in Poland. Then I left, came here. And now I'm back at thirty-seven, oldest one in the room. The students are very nice to me. Like I'm their uncle.
B: Ha, that's not a bad position to be in, to be fair. So when you're up on Dartmoor, are you just walking, or is it, like, for the course?
A: Bit of both. Erm, Dartmoor is full of Bronze Age stuff, if you know where to look. Stone rows, long lines of stones going across the moor, sometimes hundreds of metres, and nobody really knows why. And hut circles, where people lived, you can still see the rings of the walls in the grass. And the old field boundaries, reaves, they cut right across the moor. When you understand what you're looking at, it's like the whole landscape is sort of a document. Most people walk past. I don't blame them, it's raining usually.
B: Stone rows, yeah. That's brilliant, actually. We ride past Castlerigg sometimes, up near Keswick, the stone circle, and I always think I should stop and actually look at it instead of just stopping for a flapjack.
A: Castlerigg I want to see. People say it's the best setting, with the mountains round it.
B: It is, honestly. You should come up. Bring the wife, do the Lakes.
A: Hannah would like that. She likes when I plan something. I don't plan, usually.
B: I'm the opposite, I plan routes for fun. Nadia thinks it's a sickness.
A: Maybe it is. But useful sickness.
B: I'll take that. What else are you into, apart from rocks?
A: Books. Too many at once. History, and Polish science fiction, Lem mostly.
B: No way, I've got Solaris on the shelf. I've been reading loads of sci-fi lately. Haven't started that one, though, it looked a bit heavy.
A: Solaris is heavy, yeah. Start with The Cyberiad. It's robots building machines that do stupid things. It's very funny. Then Solaris, when you're ready to be sad.
B: Ready to be sad, right. Noted. Are you reading something for uni at the minute or is that all Lem?
A: I should be reading for an essay. Bronze Age burial practices. I'm behind. It's due Friday, so I'll do it Thursday night, like always.
B: Thursday night, classic. Is that the cairns and that, or —
A: Cairns, cists, barrows. There's a cist on Dartmoor, at Whitehorse Hill, they found a burial with beads and a basket, and the —
